title: Harmony and Voice Leading II: Chord Progressions and Predominant Function

guide.summary: Unit 5 expands harmonic vocabulary: predominant chords and their voice leading, root motion by fifths, six-four chord types, other diatonic progressions, and harmonic rhythm.

sections.heading: Progressions and root motion
sections.body: Strong progressions often move by descending fifths (vi–ii–V–I) or descending thirds (I–vi–IV–ii). Predominant chords (IV, ii, ii6, ii7, ii6/5) lead to dominant (V, V7, vii°6). ii6 is especially common because its bass, scale degree 4, moves up by step to 5. Retrogressions (e.g., V–IV) are generally avoided in common-practice style. The iii chord is rare and often appears in descending-bass patterns. Harmonic rhythm is the rate at which chords change; it often speeds up approaching a cadence.

sections.heading: Six-four chords and other expansions
sections.body: Second-inversion triads appear in specific patterns: the cadential 6/4 (I6/4–V, the 6 and 4 resolving down to 5 and 3), the passing 6/4 (bass moves stepwise, e.g., I – V6/4 – I6 or IV – I6/4 – IV6), the pedal or neighbor 6/4 (I – IV6/4 – I over a sustained bass), and the arpeggiated 6/4 (bass arpeggiates a sustained harmony). Tonic expansion often uses V6/4, V4/3, or vii°6 as passing chords between I and I6. In minor keys, raise the leading tone in V and vii°.

sections.heading: Harmonizing a melody
sections.body: To harmonize a melody or compose a bass line, first identify the key and cadence points, then choose chords that contain each melody note and follow the phrase model (T–PD–D–T). Aim for contrary motion between soprano and bass, avoid parallel perfect intervals between outer voices, and end with an appropriate cadence. Use inversions (I6, ii6, V6) to create a smoother, more melodic bass.

sections.heading: Worked example: harmonizing a melody
sections.body: Given the soprano C5–D5–B4–C5 in C major, find chords that contain each note. C can be I, IV, or vi; D can be ii, V, or vii°; B can be V or iii; C at the end is I. A strong choice is I–ii6–V–I or I–V6/4 (passing)–V–I, following T–PD–D–T. Then write a bass line in contrary motion to the soprano where possible, such as C3–F3–G3–C3 for I–ii6–V–I. Check outer voices for parallel perfect intervals and end with a clear cadence.

sections.heading: Common progressions to know
sections.body: Practice recognizing and writing I–IV–V–I, I–vi–ii–V–I, I–ii6–V–I, I–IV–I6/4–V–I, and I–V6–vi–IV (common in popular music). The descending fifths pattern vi–ii–V–I creates strong forward motion. Plagal and deceptive motions extend phrases.

sections.heading: Bass line composition
sections.body: When composing a bass line under a melody, use mostly stepwise motion and leaps of fourths and fifths, choose inversions to create smooth motion, and avoid repeated parallel motion with the soprano. Aim for a mix of contrary, oblique, and similar motion.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students choose chords that do not contain the melody note, use 6/4 chords outside standard patterns, and end without a proper cadence.

sections.heading: Worked example: six-four chords
sections.body: In C major, a cadential 6/4 places C and E over a G bass (I6/4) before V, with the C moving to B and the E to D. A passing 6/4 might appear in I–V6/4–I6, with the bass moving C–D–E stepwise. A pedal 6/4 appears in I–IV6/4–I, with the bass holding C while upper voices move to F and A and back. Label each type by its bass motion and function.

sections.heading: Harmonic rhythm in practice
sections.body: Composers often change chords once per measure in early phrases, then speed up the harmonic rhythm approaching a cadence. Listening for faster chord changes can help you anticipate the end of a phrase in dictation.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know predominant function, root motion, descending fifths, retrogression, the four types of six-four chords, harmonic rhythm, and bass line composition.

sections.heading: Practice routine
sections.body: Harmonize a short melody each week, trying two different chord choices for the same notes and comparing the results. Sing bass lines of common progressions to train your ear for harmonic dictation, and practice identifying six-four chords by their bass motion.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: The bass line composition or melody harmonization question asks you to choose chords and write a bass that fits a given melody. Plan the cadence first, use T–PD–D–T, prefer contrary motion with the melody, and check for parallels. Label every chord with a Roman numeral and inversion.

keyTakeaways: Four types of 6/4: cadential, passing, pedal, arpeggiated.
commonMistakes: Using a 6/4 chord outside standard patterns.
Parallel octaves between outer voices when harmonizing.
Forgetting the raised leading tone in minor.
Choosing chords that don't contain the melody note.
examTips: Plan the cadence first when harmonizing.
Use inversions for stepwise bass lines.

practice.prompt: Harmonize the soprano melody E4 – F4 – D4 – C4 in C major. Give a Roman numeral for each note and compose a bass line (pitches), ending with a perfect authentic cadence.

rubric.description: ii6 or IV (bass F2 or F3).
No parallel fifths/octaves with the soprano; ideally contrary motion.
V–I root position with soprano on tonic = PAC.

practice.sampleResponse:
Roman numerals: I – ii6 – V – I.
Bass: C3 – F2 – G2 – C3.
I (C3 under E4) moves to ii6 (F2 under F4): the bass falls while the soprano rises (contrary motion), avoiding a direct octave. ii6 (bass F, scale degree 4) rises by step to V (G2 under D4), again in contrary motion with the soprano, and V moves to I (C3 under C4). The final V–I with both chords in root position and the soprano on the tonic is a perfect authentic cadence. IV could replace ii6 for chord 2.
